1.q: רְדִ֣י ׀ וּ⁠שְׁבִ֣י & שְׁבִי & לֹ֤א תוֹסִ֨יפִי֙ יִקְרְאוּ־לָ֔⁠ךְ
1.note: The word **you** and the implied “you” in the imperatives **Come down**, **sit**, and **Sit** are feminine singular here because they refers to the **virgin of the daughter of Babylon**. The same is true of the word “your” and the implied “you” in the imperatives in verses 2 and 3. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use feminine forms if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking of Babylon’s downfall as if Babylon were a person who must **Come down and sit in the dust**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come down and be humbled]

1.q: רְדִ֣י וּ⁠שְׁבִ֣י עַל־עָפָ֗ר בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־בָּבֶ֔ל שְׁבִי־לָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ אֵין־כִּסֵּ֖א בַּת־כַּשְׂדִּ֑ים
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Come down and sit in the dust on the ground without a throne, virgin daughter of Babylon and of the Chaldeans!]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the city of Babylon as if it were a **virgin**, a young woman. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [sheltered daughter of Babylon]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Babylon losing its royal authority as if Babylon were a queen forced to **Sit on the ground without a throne**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Sit on the ground because you no longer have royal authority]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the nation of the Chaldeans as if it were a **daughter**, a young woman. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you Chaldeans]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

The terms **tender** and **delicate** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very pampered]

2.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of Babylon being reduced to the lowest status as if Babylon were a slave woman who had to **Take the millstones and grind flour**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be brought down to the lowest status of a slave]

Yahweh is referring to shameful nakedness in a polite way by using the phrase **uncover the thigh**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [expose your nakedness]

3.note: The expression **will be uncovered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Your enemies will uncover your nakedness; they will also see your reproach]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Babylon being shamed and led away into captivity as if Babylon were a woman whose **nakedness will be uncovered**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will be publicly shamed and led away into captivity]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **nakedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Your naked body]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your disgrace]

Yahweh is using **and I will not meet a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will spare no one.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will spare no one]

4.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh as if he were the people’s **Redeemer**, a relative who pays to free family members from slavery or to buy back what they have lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who frees us]
The phrase **the Holy One of Israel** is a name that refers to Yahweh, the God whom the people of Israel worship.

5.q: שְׁבִ֥י דוּמָ֛ם וּ⁠בֹ֥אִי בַ⁠חֹ֖שֶׁךְ בַּת כַּשְׂדִּ֑ים כִּ֣י לֹ֤א תוֹסִ֨יפִי֙ יִקְרְאוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ גְּבֶ֖רֶת מַמְלָכֽוֹת
5.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you will never again be called ‘The Mistress of Kingdoms’]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Babylon being defeated and taken into captivity as if Babylon were a person told to **Sit silently and go into darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be humbled and go into exile]
See how you translated the similar expression in [47:1](ta:47).

Here Yahweh is speaking of the city of Babylon as if it were **The Mistress of Kingdoms**, a queen who ruled over many other realms. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Queen Who Ruled Over All Kingdoms]

6.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an **inheritance** that is characterized by belonging to him, namely the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people who belong to me]

Here, **hand** represents “power and control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I gave them into your power]

Yahweh is using the adjective **elderly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [elderly people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the harsh oppression that Babylon imposed on the people as if it were a heavy **yoke** that Babylon placed on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you oppressed them very harshly]

7.note: Here Babylon is speaking of itself as if it were a **mistress**, a queen who would rule over others forever. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will always rule over others]

Yahweh uses the word **yet** here to indicate a contrast between Babylon’s claim that she would rule forever and her failure to consider what would happen to her. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but]

Here, **heart** represents “thoughts and attention.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you did not give any thought to these things]
The pronoun **these** refers to the things Yahweh has been saying about Babylon’s coming downfall. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these warnings]
The pronoun **its** refers to what would finally happen to Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the prophesied outcome] or [your end]

8.note: Yahweh is using the adjective **luxuriant** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [one who lives in luxury]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who dwells securely]
Here, **heart** represents “inner thoughts.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Babylon saying to herself]

Babylon is using **and besides me there is none** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there is no one else as great as I am.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is no one else as great as I am] or [there is no one who compares to me]

Here Babylon is speaking of losing her king and protectors as if she were a woman who would become a **widow**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not lose my king]

Here Babylon is speaking of losing her people as if she were a mother who would suffer **bereavement**, the loss of her children. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will not lose my children]

9.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
The pronoun **these** refers to bereavement and widowhood, which Yahweh names later in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [two things will come to]

The terms **bereavement** and **widowhood** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the complete loss of your family]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [In their full measure]

10.note: Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the judgment he has just announced and Babylon’s confidence in her own wickedness and wisdom. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, you trusted]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in your wicked deeds]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Your wisdom and your knowledge** with the information about how it **led you astray**. Alternate translation: [Your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **knowledge**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [How wise you are and what you know]

The terms **wisdom** and **knowledge** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Your great wisdom]

Yahweh is using **it led you astray** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it caused you to make a serious mistake.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it caused you to make a serious mistake]
Here, **heart** represents “inner thoughts.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you said in your mind]
See how you translated the similar expression in 47:8.

11.q: וּ⁠בָ֧א עָלַ֣יִ⁠ךְ רָעָ֗ה לֹ֤א תֵדְעִי֙ שַׁחְרָ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠תִפֹּ֤ל עָלַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ & הֹוָ֔ה לֹ֥א & תוּכְלִ֖י כַּפְּרָ֑⁠הּ וְ⁠תָבֹ֨א עָלַ֧יִ⁠ךְ & פִּתְאֹ֛ם שׁוֹאָ֖ה לֹ֥א & תֵדָֽעִי
11.note: These three clauses mean basically the same thing. The second and third emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including all three phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second and third phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And trouble will come upon you; you will not know its dawning. Yes, ruin will fall upon you; you will not be able to atone for it. Yes, desolation will come upon you suddenly; you will not know] or [Trouble, ruin, and desolation will come upon you without warning and without relief]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [things that trouble you]
The pronoun **its** refers to the trouble that will come upon Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the dawning of the trouble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a devastating blow]

12.note: The terms **spells** and **sorceries** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with all your magical arts]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **sorceries** that are characterized by being performed by Babylon. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with the many sorceries you practice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **youth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from when you were young]

13.note: The expression **have been tired** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The abundance of your counsels has wearied you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsels**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by the many who counsel you]

Here Isaiah is introducing Babylon’s astrologers, referred to here as **them**, as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Let your astrologers stand, please, and save you]

The phrases **the dividers of the heavens** and **the seers of the stars** describe astrologers, people who studied the sky and the stars in order to predict future events. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the name of a similar kind of person that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the astrologers, the stargazers]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **stubble** is quickly and completely burned up by fire, so will **they** be destroyed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like stubble, they will be completely destroyed]
The pronoun **they** refers to the astrologers Babylon relied on. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those astrologers will become like stubble]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the destruction of the astrologers as if **fire will burn them up** like dry plants. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will be completely destroyed]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **souls**, or lives, that are characterized by belonging to the astrologers themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the lives that belong to them]

Here, **hand** represents “the power of the flame.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of the flame]

15.note: The word translated as **Thus** indicates that what follows is a result or summary of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Therefore]
The pronoun **they** refers to the astrologers and merchants whom Babylon relied on. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those astrologers will become for you]
Alternate translation: [Each man will wander to his own side]

Yahweh is using **A man to his side they will wander** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each of them will go off in his own direction.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each of them will go off in his own direction]

Yahweh is using the singular noun **man** to mean each person individually. Your language may use a singular noun in the same way. If not, you can translate this with an equivalent phrase such as “each one.” Alternate translation: [Each one to his own direction]
